card: After a number, the noun's form depends on the **last word** of the number: **1** → nominative singular (**оди́н стол**), **2, 3, 4** → genitive singular (**два стола́**), **5–20** and anything ending in 0, 5–9 → genitive plural (**пять столо́в**). So **21 стол**, **22 стола́**, **25 столо́в**.

table.caption: Compound numbers simply line up: 345 = **три́ста со́рок пять**.

sections.body: The 2–4 rule is a fossil. Old Russian had a *dual* number for pairs of things, and **два стола́** is that old dual ending, which happens to look like the genitive singular today. Three and four followed two. From five upwards, numbers were originally nouns (*a five of tables*), so they took the genitive plural like **мно́го столо́в**.

sections.title: Gender in 1 and 2
sections.body:
**оди́н** agrees like an adjective: **оди́н стол**, **одна́ кни́га**, **одно́ окно́**. **два** has a feminine form **две**: **два стола́, два окна́**, but **две кни́ги**. From three on there is no gender.

The teens all have their stress on **-на́-**: **пятна́дцать**, **семна́дцать**, except **оди́ннадцать** and **четы́рнадцать**.

sections.title: Years: год, го́да, лет
sections.body: Age and durations are the commonest place to meet this rule: **оди́н год**, **два го́да**, **пять лет**, **два́дцать оди́н год**, **два́дцать два го́да**, **два́дцать пять лет**. **лет** is the genitive plural of **год**, borrowed from **ле́то** (*summer*). With age, the person is dative: **Мне три́дцать лет.**
Remember the shopping list: **оди́н рубль**, **два рубля́**, **пять рубле́й**. Every price you hear in Russia rehearses the rule.

mistakes.why: 5 and above take the genitive plural; for **год** that is **лет**.

examples.ru: У меня́ два бра́та и одна́ сестра́.
examples.en: I have two brothers and one sister.
I've been waiting for ten minutes.
We were there for two days.
